flows.title: Very low resistance from main rail to ground
flows.symptomDescription: Input voltage correct externally → Connect motherboard → Adapter protection trips → or excessive current occurs
flows.hypothesis: Component on main rail has failed short
flows.test: POWER REMOVED: Measure resistance from main rail to ground
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → Shorted load / → MOSFET / capacitor → Find short → Replace failed component
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → Input control / → sequencing fault
flows.notes: Electrical overstress failures can manifest as excessive supply current, low resistance from supply to ground, or shorted supply pins. Resistance measurements must be performed with power removed.
references: Reference: Infineon — Electrical Over-Stress (EOS): Review and FAQ.

flows.title: One required power rail is completely missing
flows.symptomDescription: Examples might include a CPU, memory, PCH, GPU, or auxiliary rail, depending on the platform.
flows.hypothesis: Rail regulator is not being enabled
flows.test: Measure regulator EN / ENABLE signal
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → Regulator / MOSFET / → load problem → Check regulator → Find cause → Repair
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → Earlier sequencing → stage not satisfied
flows.notes: This is an important diagnostic distinction: The controller may simply never receive permission to turn on. Power-management systems commonly use enable, sequencing, supervision, and reset logic to determine when downstream rails may start.
references: References: Texas Instruments — Creating a Sequencing Voltage Supervisor; TI — TLV840 voltage-supervisor documentation.
rawFlow: Rail regulator is not being enabled

flows.title: RAIL APPEARS THEN DISAPPEARS
flows.symptomDescription: Press Power → Rail rises → Rail immediately falls to 0 V
flows.hypothesis: Regulator protection is activating because of excessive load
flows.test: Measure resistance from that rail to ground with power removed
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → Short / heavy load → Find short → Repair
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → Enable / PGOOD / → regulator failure
flows.notes: Protection circuits are specifically designed to react to conditions such as overcurrent and short circuits, so a rail that immediately collapses does not necessarily mean the regulator itself failed.

flows.title: VRM AREA GETS HOT VERY QUICKLY
flows.sourceSection: 7. VRM AREA GETS HOT VERY QUICKLY
flows.symptomDescription: Power ON → VRM component heats rapidly → System shuts down / rail abnormal
flows.hypothesis: VRM is supplying excessive current into a shorted load
flows.test: POWER REMOVED: Measure rail-to-ground resistance
flows.yesOutcome: Investigate load → short → Find component → Repair
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → MOSFET switching / → regulator fault
flows.notes: Do not assume: A regulator or MOSFET may simply be getting hot because a downstream component is drawing excessive current.

flows.title: STANDBY / ALWAYS-ON RAIL MISSING
flows.symptomDescription: A completely dead motherboard often makes this one of the highest-value early tests.
flows.hypothesis: Always-on rail is absent
flows.test: Measure ONE expected standby rail
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → power-button / → sequencing logic
flows.noOutcome: Narrow down → Standby regulator → or supply path → Find cause → Repair

flows.title: POWER RAIL TOO LOW OR UNSTABLE
flows.sourceSection: 9. POWER RAIL TOO LOW OR UNSTABLE
flows.symptomDescription: Expected rail → ≈ correct nominal voltage → Measured rail → = low / fluctuating
flows.hypothesis: Excessive load is pulling rail down
flows.test: Measure resistance of that rail to ground with power removed
flows.yesOutcome: Load-side fault → Find load → Repair
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → regulator / feedback
rawFlow: Excessive load is pulling rail down

flows.title: POWER RAIL SHORTED TO GROUND
flows.symptomDescription: Rail resistance → Near-short / unexpectedly low
flows.hypothesis: One component connected to rail has failed short
flows.test: Isolate ONE branch/component from the rail
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → Fault lies on → isolated branch → Find component → Replace component
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → Another branch → contains fault
flows.notes: This method is usually more defensible than randomly removing capacitors.

flows.title: MOSFET SHORTED DRAIN-TO-SOURCE
flows.symptomDescription: Suspected rail short → MOSFET area identified → Unexpectedly low D-S resistance
flows.hypothesis: MOSFET has internally failed Drain-to-Source
flows.test: POWER REMOVED: Check D-S resistance / diode behavior
flows.yesOutcome: MOSFET strongly → suspect → Find cause → Replace only after → root cause assessment
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → downstream short / → gate-control fault
flows.notes: MOSFET failures can produce low-resistance shorts between terminals, but a failed MOSFET may itself be the result of overcurrent, shoot-through, excessive voltage, or another upstream/downstream fault. Simply replacing it without identifying why it failed can lead to repeat failure.

flows.title: INPUT MOSFET DOES NOT TURN ON
flows.sourceSection: 12. INPUT MOSFET DOES NOT TURN ON
flows.symptomDescription: Voltage at MOSFET input → = correct → Voltage at output → = 0 V
flows.hypothesis: Gate is not being driven correctly
flows.test: Measure VGS Gate-to-Source voltage
flows.yesOutcome: MOSFET itself → suspect → Test MOSFET → Repair
flows.noOutcome: Gate driver / → controller / → protection logic
flows.notes: This is a much better test than: because MOSFET conduction depends on its gate-drive condition.
rawFlow: Gate is not being driven correctly

flows.title: SHORTED CAPACITOR ON A POWER RAIL
flows.sourceSection: 13. SHORTED CAPACITOR ON A POWER RAIL
flows.symptomDescription: Rail short to ground → Many parallel capacitors → connected to same rail
flows.hypothesis: One decoupling capacitor has failed short
flows.test: Isolate ONE suspected capacitor
flows.yesOutcome: Capacitor identified → Replace capacitor
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → Test next branch / → component
flows.notes: The major trap here is that every capacitor connected to a shorted rail will appear connected to the short. That does not mean every capacitor is defective.

flows.title: CAPACITOR / FILTERING PROBLEM — UNSTABLE RAIL
flows.symptomDescription: Rail exists → but → voltage unstable / excessive ripple
flows.hypothesis: Output filtering is defective
flows.test: Measure rail waveform with oscilloscope
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → capacitor / ESR / → feedback network → Find cause → Repair
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → regulator / → load transient
flows.notes: A multimeter can show average voltage while completely hiding fast ripple or oscillation, so an oscilloscope becomes the appropriate tool once the problem is suspected to be dynamic.

flows.title: Switching activity before the coil, but no proper voltage after it
flows.symptomDescription: VRM controller active → Switching node activity present → Output rail absent
flows.hypothesis: Inductor connection is open / damaged
flows.test: POWER REMOVED: Check continuity across inductor
flows.yesOutcome: Inductor / solder → joint fault → Repair
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → MOSFET / → feedback / load
flows.notes: An inductor in a buck regulator is part of the energy-transfer and output-filter path, so an open connection can prevent the expected output from reaching the rail.

flows.title: CHIPSET / PCH INITIALIZATION STOPS
flows.symptomDescription: Input power good → Standby rails good → Main rails appear good → System still does not progress → toward POST
flows.symptom: Power rails appear valid but initialization stops
flows.hypothesis: PCH / platform controller is not receiving required clock / reset / power-good condition
flows.test: Check ONE required control signal for example RESET or PWRGOOD
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → clock / firmware / → CPU / PCH
flows.noOutcome: Trace previous → sequencing stage → Find cause → Repair
flows.notes: Do not jump directly to “bad PCH.” A PCH that appears inactive may simply be waiting for a missing prerequisite such as power-good, reset release, a clock, or another sequenced rail. Intel platform documentation shows that power, clocks, reset and PWRGOOD are explicitly related during initialization.

flows.title: REQUIRED CLOCK MISSING
flows.symptomDescription: Power rails present → System does not initialize → Required clock absent
flows.hypothesis: Clock generator / oscillator is not operating
flows.test: Measure ONE required clock with suitable oscilloscope/probe
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → clock source / → enable / supply → Find cause → Repair
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → reset / → downstream logic
flows.notes: Processor/platform startup depends on valid clocks as well as supplies. Intel describes PWRGOOD as indicating that required clocks and supplies are stable and within specification.

flows.title: RESET SIGNAL NEVER RELEASES
flows.symptomDescription: Rails stable → Clock present → RESET remains active → No initialization
flows.hypothesis: Reset controller is waiting for a prerequisite rail/signal
flows.test: Check ONE prerequisite Power-Good signal
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → reset controller / → downstream logic
flows.noOutcome: Trace failed rail → or supervisor → Find cause → Repair
flows.notes: Voltage-supervisor devices are specifically designed to monitor rails and control reset behavior.
references: References: Texas Instruments — Voltage Supervisor and Reset IC documentation.

flows.title: PWRGOOD NEVER ASSERTS
flows.symptomDescription: This is one of the most important signals in advanced motherboard troubleshooting. → Major rails appear present → System does not advance → PWRGOOD remains inactive
flows.hypothesis: One required supply or clock has not reached valid condition
flows.test: Check ONE rail monitored before PWRGOOD assertion
flows.yesOutcome: Test next → prerequisite
flows.noOutcome: Narrow down → failed rail → Find cause → Repair
flows.notes: Intel defines PWRGOOD as an indication that processor clocks and power supplies are stable and within specification. It must remain inactive until those conditions are valid.

flows.title: No POST after CPU installation or replacement
flows.symptomDescription: CPU installed / upgraded → Power ON → Fans / power present → No POST
flows.hypothesis: CPU is not supported by the current motherboard configuration
flows.test: Check motherboard CPU-support list against installed BIOS version
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → CPU seating / → socket / CPU fault → Continue hardware → diagnosis → Find cause → Repair
flows.noOutcome: Narrow down → BIOS compatibility → problem → Move to Layer 4 → BIOS update
flows.notes: This distinction is critical. A perfectly functional CPU may fail to boot if the motherboard firmware does not support that processor. AMD explicitly documents cases where a compatible motherboard requires a BIOS update before a newer processor can boot.
references: References: AMD — Unable to Boot New Desktop System Configured with AMD Ryzen Processor; AMD — Troubleshooting Common Boot Failures.

flows.title: System crashes, freezes, or fails under CPU load
flows.symptomDescription: Idle → stable → CPU-heavy workload → crash / freeze / reboot
flows.hypothesis: CPU is unstable or defective
flows.test: Run processor-specific diagnostic / stress test
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → CPU / CPU power / → thermal condition → Find cause → Repair
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → RAM / cooling / → motherboard / software
flows.notes: Intel's Processor Diagnostic Tool verifies processor functionality, operating frequency, processor features, cores, and includes a stress test. A failed CPU stress test is useful evidence, but it does not by itself prove the silicon is defective because cooling or power delivery can also cause failure under load.
references: Reference: Intel — Intel Processor Diagnostic Tool.

flows.title: CPU performance becomes unexpectedly slow under load
flows.symptomDescription: Heavy workload → CPU frequency falls → Performance becomes very low
flows.hypothesis: CPU is thermal throttling
flows.test: Monitor CPU temperature during the same workload
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → Cooling system → problem → Move to Cooling → Find cause → Repair
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → power limit / → configuration / → software
flows.notes: Modern Intel processors reduce performance when thermal limits are reached and can automatically shut down if throttling cannot control temperature.
references: Reference: Intel — Why Does Intel Core Processor Enable Throttling While Gaming?

flows.title: No POST with memory error indication
flows.symptomDescription: Power ON → No POST → Memory LED / → beep code / → diagnostic code
flows.hypothesis: One RAM module is defective
flows.test: Boot using ONE RAM module only in the recommended slot
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → Removed RAM / → configuration → suspect → Test modules individually → Find failed module → Replace
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → remaining module / → slot / CPU IMC
flows.notes: Dell recommends testing memory modules individually and observing whether the failure follows a specific SO-DIMM or remains associated with a particular socket.
references: Reference: Dell — How to Diagnose and Resolve Common Memory Issues.
rawFlow: Boot using ONE RAM module only

flows.title: RANDOM CRASHES / MEMORY ERRORS
flows.symptomDescription: System boots → Random: → freezes → STOP errors → application crashes → data errors
flows.hypothesis: RAM contains memory errors
flows.test: Run extended hardware memory diagnostic
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → RAM / memory slot → Isolate module → Find cause → Replace / repair
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → CPU / software / → storage / GPU
flows.notes: Dell lists startup failures, STOP errors, freezes, read errors, and application problems among common symptoms of memory faults, and recommends hardware memory diagnostics.

flows.title: INCORRECT MEMORY CAPACITY
flows.symptomDescription: Installed → 32 GB RAM → System detects → 16 GB
flows.symptom: Installed RAM capacity not fully detected
flows.hypothesis: One memory module is not being detected
flows.test: Boot with the suspect module alone
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → slot / configuration
flows.noOutcome: Module suspect → Test known-good → replacement → Find cause → Repair
flows.notes: Testing modules individually is an effective method for determining whether the problem follows a DIMM/SO-DIMM or the motherboard socket.

flows.title: RAM works in one slot but not another
flows.symptomDescription: RAM A + Slot 1 → POST → Same RAM A + Slot 2 → No POST
flows.symptom: Same module behaves differently between slots
flows.hypothesis: Memory slot / channel path is defective
flows.test: Install known-good RAM in suspect slot
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → slot / channel fault → Inspect slot / CPU → socket / board path → Find cause → Repair
flows.noOutcome: RAM module / → seating issue
flows.notes: Dell specifically states that if a fault consistently remains with a particular slot rather than following the memory module, the slot or associated motherboard path has been isolated as the suspect. On many modern CPUs: Therefore: CPU/socket contact problems can also affect memory channels.

flows.title: No display from motherboard video output
flows.symptomDescription: System powers on → Monitor connected → to motherboard HDMI/DP → No image
flows.hypothesis: Installed CPU does not provide integrated graphics
flows.test: Check exact CPU specification for integrated graphics support
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → display path / → firmware / iGPU
flows.noOutcome: Cause identified → Use discrete GPU
flows.notes: AMD explicitly warns that motherboard display outputs require a processor with integrated graphics support. A motherboard HDMI connector does not mean every installed processor can generate video through it.
references: Reference: AMD — Troubleshooting Common Boot Failures.

flows.title: INTEGRATED GRAPHICS DISPLAY INSTABILITY
flows.symptomDescription: iGPU display works → Flickering / corruption / → black screen occurs
flows.hypothesis: Display output path is causing the symptom
flows.test: Connect a known-good external display/cable
flows.yesOutcome: iGPU/platform suspect → Continue graphics → diagnosis → Find cause → Repair
flows.noOutcome: Display/cable/ → panel path
flows.notes: A display-path test prevents incorrectly diagnosing the iGPU when the actual problem is the panel, cable, monitor, or output connection. AMD recommends verifying the monitor, cable, input selection, and graphics output when diagnosing no-display conditions.

flows.title: DEDICATED GPU — NO DISPLAY
flows.symptomDescription: Power ON → System appears to run → Discrete GPU installed → No display
flows.hypothesis: Dedicated GPU is defective
flows.test: Replace ONLY the GPU with known-good compatible GPU
flows.yesOutcome: Original GPU suspect → Find cause → Repair / replace
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → motherboard / → PSU / POST / → display path
flows.notes: AMD recommends a swap test with a known-working graphics card; if the system displays correctly with the replacement, the original card becomes the primary suspect.
references: Reference: AMD — Troubleshooting Common Boot Failures.

flows.title: DEDICATED GPU — ARTIFACTS
flows.symptomDescription: Display present → Colored blocks → lines → random pixels → texture corruption
flows.hypothesis: Dedicated GPU hardware is causing artifacts
flows.test: Substitute known-good GPU
flows.yesOutcome: Original GPU isolated → GPU / VRAM / board → Find cause → Repair / replace
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → monitor / cable / → software / RAM
flows.notes: A GPU swap test is stronger evidence than judging artifacts visually because similar corruption can arise from the display path or software. AMD's hardware troubleshooting process recommends known-good GPU substitution when isolating graphics failures.

flows.title: GPU CRASHES UNDER LOAD
flows.symptomDescription: Desktop usage → stable → 3D game / rendering → black screen / → crash / reboot
flows.hypothesis: Dedicated GPU becomes unstable under load
flows.test: Run equivalent workload with known-good GPU
flows.yesOutcome: Original GPU suspect → Inspect GPU cooling → or replace → Find cause → Repair
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → PSU / CPU / → RAM / software
flows.notes: Do not immediately call this “GPU failure.” A load-related reboot can also originate from PSU, temperature, RAM, or software, so substitution is a cleaner isolation test.

flows.title: CPU temperature rises abnormally fast
flows.symptomDescription: System starts → CPU temperature → rises rapidly → Throttling / shutdown
flows.hypothesis: Heatsink is not making proper contact with CPU
flows.test: Inspect heatsink mounting and physical contact
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → mounting problem → Reinstall cooler → Repair
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → fan / thermal → interface / load
flows.notes: Intel identifies incorrect thermal-solution assembly as a condition capable of causing thermal throttling and automatic shutdown.

flows.title: COOLING FAN DOES NOT SPIN
flows.symptomDescription: System ON → Temperature increases → Cooling fan remains stopped
flows.hypothesis: Fan assembly has failed
flows.test: Connect known-good compatible fan
flows.yesOutcome: Original fan fault → Replace fan
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → fan power / → controller / → motherboard
flows.notes: A non-operating cooling system can lead to overheating, throttling, and shutdown; Intel documents throttling and automatic shutdown as processor thermal-protection mechanisms.

flows.title: FAN CONSTANTLY RUNNING AT HIGH SPEED
flows.sourceSection: 13. FAN CONSTANTLY RUNNING AT HIGH SPEED
flows.symptomDescription: Low system load → Fan continuously → near maximum speed
flows.hypothesis: CPU temperature is actually too high
flows.test: Measure CPU temperature at idle
flows.yesOutcome: Cooling problem → Check heatsink / → thermal interface → Find cause → Repair
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → fan control / → firmware / → sensor behavior
flows.notes: The important point is that loud fan operation is a response, not automatically a fan defect.

flows.title: High temperatures after heatsink installation
flows.symptomDescription: Cooler removed / → CPU serviced → Cooler reinstalled → Temperature now → much higher than before
flows.hypothesis: Thermal interface / cooler contact is incorrect
flows.test: Remove cooler and inspect thermal-contact pattern
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → TIM / mounting → problem → Clean and reinstall → with correct TIM
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → fan / heatsink / → power configuration
flows.notes: Incorrect thermal-solution assembly can cause processors to reach their thermal limits, triggering throttling or automatic shutdown.

flows.title: No POST after failed or interrupted BIOS update
flows.symptomDescription: System worked normally → BIOS update started → Update failed / power lost / → system interrupted → Restart → Black screen / no POST / → diagnostic LED / boot loop
flows.symptom: No POST immediately after failed BIOS update
flows.hypothesis: BIOS firmware image is corrupted
flows.test: Attempt manufacturer-supported BIOS Recovery procedure
flows.observe: Recovery environment starts and firmware restores?
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → Firmware corruption → confirmed → Recover firmware → Find cause → Repair
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → recovery image / → flash storage / → motherboard path
flows.notes: Dell specifically lists symptoms such as no POST, black screen, repeated restarts, BIOS-corruption messages, and certain diagnostic LED patterns as situations where BIOS Recovery may be appropriate. HP also provides BIOS recovery procedures for systems affected by BIOS corruption.
references: References: Dell — BIOS Recovery; HP — Recovering the BIOS.

flows.title: System repeatedly restarts before POST completes
flows.symptomDescription: Press Power → Fans / LEDs start → No normal POST → Restart → Same cycle repeats
flows.hypothesis: Stored BIOS configuration or firmware is corrupted
flows.test: Clear CMOS / restore firmware defaults using manufacturer procedure
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → Invalid/corrupt → configuration → Reconfigure BIOS
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → BIOS firmware / → Layer 2 / Layer 3
flows.notes: Clearing CMOS is a legitimate recovery step for certain no-boot/no-display conditions, but the exact procedure is model-specific. Intel and HP both document CMOS reset procedures as troubleshooting or BIOS-recovery steps. Important: A boot loop can also originate from power sequencing, RAM, CPU, or other hardware. The timing and diagnostic indicators determine which layer should be investigated.

flows.title: FAILURE AFTER BIOS SETTING CHANGE
flows.symptomDescription: System worked → BIOS setting changed → Save & Restart → No POST / unstable startup / → hardware no longer detected → Examples may include aggressive memory configuration, CPU settings, storage configuration, or other platform-specific settings.
flows.symptom: Failure starts immediately after BIOS configuration change
flows.hypothesis: New firmware configuration is invalid / unstable
flows.test: Clear CMOS / load firmware defaults
flows.yesOutcome: Configuration fault → Identify changed → setting → Correct configuration
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → firmware / → hardware fault
flows.notes: CMOS reset returns stored configuration toward platform defaults and is therefore a useful isolation test when a configuration change immediately precedes the failure.

flows.title: BIOS recovery repeatedly fails
flows.symptomDescription: BIOS corruption suspected → Correct recovery image used → Manufacturer recovery starts → Recovery repeatedly fails → or cannot complete
flows.hypothesis: Firmware storage / write path may be faulty
flows.test: Attempt ONE known-valid manufacturer recovery image
flows.yesOutcome: Firmware image fixed
flows.noOutcome: Narrow down → flash chip /
flows.notes: Do not immediately replace the flash IC merely because normal BIOS recovery fails. The recovery image, firmware version, recovery mechanism, power integrity, and flash-access circuitry must also be considered. Manufacturer BIOS Recovery should normally be attempted before chip-level intervention.

flows.title: Advanced board-level diagnosis
flows.sourceSection: 5. BIOS FLASH CONTENT CANNOT BE VERIFIED
flows.symptomDescription: Firmware recovery fails → Other major hardware → appears functional → BIOS flash storage suspected
flows.hypothesis: Firmware contents are corrupt or flash device cannot reliably retain data
flows.test: Read flash contents using a suitable external programmer
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → firmware image / → configuration / → another subsystem
flows.noOutcome: Flash device / → circuit suspect → Investigate supply, → SPI lines, flash IC → Find cause → Repair / reprogram → Read-back verification → Reinstall
flows.notes: This is advanced repair, not an early troubleshooting step. A better escalation path is: Firmware is stored in firmware volumes from which initialization components and DXE drivers are discovered and executed during platform initialization.

flows.title: Date and time reset after power removal
flows.symptomDescription: Set correct date/time → Shutdown → Remove AC power → Wait → Start computer → Date/time incorrect again
flows.hypothesis: RTC / CMOS backup battery cannot maintain RTC state
flows.test: Measure / replace with known-good correct RTC battery
flows.yesOutcome: Battery fault → confirmed → Replace battery
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → RTC circuit / → board issue
flows.notes: Dell diagnostic documentation explicitly associates RTC power failure with CMOS-battery problems on applicable desktop models.

flows.title: BIOS SETTINGS REPEATEDLY RESET
flows.symptomDescription: Change BIOS settings → Save → Power removed → Restart → Settings returned to defaults
flows.hypothesis: RTC / CMOS backup power is failing
flows.test: Replace RTC battery with known-good battery
flows.yesOutcome: Battery fault → Replace permanently
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → NVRAM / → firmware / → motherboard
flows.notes: CMOS data holds firmware settings on platforms that use this mechanism, and HP documents corrupted CMOS data as one reason a CMOS reset may be required during BIOS recovery.

flows.title: CMOS CHECKSUM / RTC ERROR
flows.symptomDescription: Power ON → POST message: → CMOS checksum error → RTC error → Time-of-day error → or CMOS reset notification
flows.hypothesis: Stored firmware configuration is invalid
flows.test: Load BIOS defaults / perform manufacturer CMOS reset
flows.yesOutcome: Configuration issue → Reconfigure settings
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → RTC battery / → RTC hardware
flows.notes: HP specifically documents BIOS ROM/CMOS checksum errors and recommends restoring defaults and investigating the CMOS battery where appropriate.

flows.title: Beep code / diagnostic LED during POST
flows.symptomDescription: Power ON → No normal boot → Beep pattern → or LED blink pattern
flows.hypothesis: POST detected failure in subsystem indicated by code
flows.test: Decode exact pattern using MODEL-SPECIFIC service manual
flows.observe: Which subsystem is indicated?  RAM / CPU / BIOS / GPU / RTC / motherboard
flows.notes: Dell documents beep and LED codes for failures including BIOS ROM, memory, chipset, RTC, video, and CPU. Importantly, Dell notes that diagnostic LEDs indicate where POST encountered difficulty; they do not by themselves prove the root cause. That distinction should be built into your database:

flows.title: POST HANGS AT LOGO
flows.symptomDescription: Power ON → Manufacturer logo appears → POST stops / freezes → No Boot Manager
flows.hypothesis: Firmware is waiting on hardware initialization
flows.test: Disconnect ONE non-essential device
flows.yesOutcome: Device / initialization → path isolated → Investigate device → Repair / replace
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → next device / → firmware stage
flows.notes: This is where ONE test becomes especially important. Do not do: Instead: UEFI DXE is responsible for initializing platform components, console devices, and boot devices, so a firmware-stage hang can occur while firmware is attempting to initialize or connect a device.

flows.title: POST SUCCEEDS BUT NO BOOT DEVICE IS SELECTED
flows.sourceSection: 11. POST SUCCEEDS BUT NO BOOT DEVICE IS SELECTED
flows.symptomDescription: POST completes → BIOS Setup accessible → Storage hardware detected → "No Boot Device" → or Boot Manager cannot select OS
flows.symptom: Drive detected but no boot occurs
flows.hypothesis: UEFI boot configuration is incorrect
flows.test: Check UEFI Boot Manager for expected OS boot entry
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → bootloader / → EFI partition
flows.noOutcome: Boot configuration → problem → Repair boot entry
flows.verify: SSD absent from firmware Hardware / initialization issue SSD detected but UEFI boot entry incorrect Layer 4 Correct UEFI boot entry but bootloader damaged Layer 5
flows.notes: The UEFI Boot Manager determines which drivers and applications—including OS bootloaders—are loaded and follows firmware boot configuration stored in UEFI variables. This is also a major Layer 4 → Layer 5 boundary:

flows.title: INCORRECT BOOT ORDER
flows.symptomDescription: System POSTs normally → Correct drive detected → Firmware tries wrong → disk / USB / network device
flows.hypothesis: Boot order is incorrect
flows.test: Place intended OS Boot Manager first in boot order
flows.yesOutcome: Boot-order fault → Save configuration
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → EFI boot entry / → bootloader / → storage
flows.notes: The UEFI specification defines boot-order variables that determine the sequence in which boot options are attempted, and HP similarly documents changing the system BIOS boot order when the wrong device is selected.

flows.title: SECURE BOOT / UEFI CONFIGURATION PREVENTS BOOT
flows.sourceSection: 13. SECURE BOOT / UEFI CONFIGURATION PREVENTS BOOT
flows.symptomDescription: System previously booted → Secure Boot / → UEFI configuration changed → Bootloader no longer starts
flows.symptom: Boot failure starts after Secure Boot change
flows.hypothesis: UEFI security policy rejects bootloader
flows.test: Restore the previously working Secure Boot setting
flows.yesOutcome: Secure Boot policy → identified → Correct Secure Boot → configuration
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → bootloader / → storage
flows.verify: Boot failure Disable Secure Boot permanently
flows.notes: Secure Boot uses UEFI trust databases and keys to determine whether boot components are accepted. Microsoft documents that the appropriate UEFI signature database and keys are required for Windows Secure Boot operation. Do not make the common mistake: That may hide a configuration or bootloader problem rather than diagnose it.

flows.title: NEW HARDWARE NOT INITIALIZED
flows.symptomDescription: Install new CPU / RAM / → PCIe device → Power available → Hardware physically compatible → POST fails or device missing
flows.hypothesis: Current firmware does not support / configure hardware correctly
flows.test: Check exact firmware version against manufacturer compatibility information
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → Layer 3 hardware / → configuration
flows.noOutcome: Firmware compatibility → issue → Update firmware → using supported method
flows.notes: This case illustrates why firmware belongs in its own layer: firmware drivers are responsible for initializing processor, chipset, platform devices, and boot devices during the DXE phase.

flows.title: POST HANGS ONLY WHEN A DEVICE IS CONNECTED
flows.sourceSection: 15. POST HANGS ONLY WHEN A DEVICE IS CONNECTED
flows.symptomDescription: Device disconnected → POST succeeds → Device connected → POST hangs
flows.symptom: POST failure follows one connected device
flows.hypothesis: Firmware cannot correctly initialize that device
flows.test: Reconnect ONLY that device to known-good interface
flows.yesOutcome: Device / firmware → interaction isolated → Check compatibility → Update / replace / → reconfigure
flows.noOutcome: Original port / → connection suspect
flows.notes: Again: The problem may be: UEFI's DXE drivers are responsible for platform and device initialization before boot-device selection.

flows.title: FIRMWARE INITIALIZATION STOPS BEFORE BOOT MANAGER
flows.sourceSection: 16. FIRMWARE INITIALIZATION STOPS BEFORE BOOT MANAGER
flows.symptomDescription: Power rails good → CPU/RAM basic hardware appears good → Firmware begins execution → System never reaches → Boot Manager
flows.hypothesis: Initialization stops during PEI / DXE
flows.test: Use available POST diagnostic code / debug output
flows.notes: UEFI PI defines distinct initialization stages. PEI establishes sufficient system state and permanent memory for DXE; DXE then initializes the processor, chipset, platform components, consoles, and boot devices before transferring toward Boot Device Selection.

flows.title: HDD absent from BIOS/UEFI storage list
flows.symptomDescription: Power ON → POST completes → Enter BIOS / UEFI → HDD not detected
flows.hypothesis: HDD itself has failed
flows.test: Connect the HDD to a known-good compatible system
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → Original SATA path → or motherboard port → Test interface → Find cause → Repair
flows.noOutcome: Narrow down → HDD strongly suspect → Run manufacturer → diagnostic if possible → Find cause → Replace drive
flows.notes: Intel's SSD troubleshooting guidance uses exactly this type of substitution logic: test the storage device in another system and test another known-good device in the original system. Intel
rawFlow: Original SATA path HDD strongly suspect

flows.title: HDD ABNORMAL CLICKING / MECHANICAL SYMPTOMS
flows.symptomDescription: HDD powered → Repeated clicking / → spin-up retry / → mechanical noise → Drive inaccessible → or unstable
flows.hypothesis: Mechanical HDD failure
flows.test: Run manufacturer non-destructive diagnostic if drive remains accessible
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → Drive failure → Backup data → if still accessible → Replace drive
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → cable / → interface / → power
flows.notes: Seagate recommends SeaTools for assessing drive health, including HDD testing and SMART-related diagnostics. Seagate If a mechanically failing HDD contains valuable data, continued testing can increase risk. Diagnose enough to identify the failure, then prioritize data recovery.

flows.title: HDD / SSD FAILS HEALTH DIAGNOSTIC
flows.symptomDescription: Drive detected → System boots sometimes → Slow reads / errors / → SMART warning
flows.hypothesis: Drive media / internal hardware is degrading
flows.test: Run manufacturer drive diagnostic
flows.yesOutcome: Drive strongly → suspect → Back up data → Replace drive
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → filesystem / → cable / → OS
flows.notes: Seagate states that a SMART error indicates an underlying drive problem and recommends running SeaTools; an underlying SMART failure is generally not something software can repair. Seagate

flows.title: SATA SSD NOT DETECTED
flows.symptomDescription: SATA SSD installed → BIOS / UEFI → SSD absent
flows.hypothesis: SSD itself is defective
flows.test: Connect SSD to another known-good SATA interface
flows.yesOutcome: Original interface → suspect → Check cable / port → Find cause → Repair
flows.noOutcome: SSD strongly → suspect → Confirm with → known-good system → Replace if failed
flows.notes: Intel recommends testing the SSD in another system, trying a known-good SSD, checking cables, and using the correct storage connector. Intel

flows.title: SATA SSD INTERMITTENTLY DISAPPEARS
flows.symptomDescription: SSD normally detected → Randomly disappears → Restart → May return
flows.hypothesis: SATA connection is unstable
flows.test: Replace ONLY the SATA data cable
flows.yesOutcome: Cable fault → isolated → Replace cable
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → SATA port / → SSD / → power
flows.notes: Crucial recommends checking connections and trying another SATA cable when isolating SSD recognition problems. Crucial

flows.title: SSD DETECTED BUT READ/WRITE ACCESS IS UNSTABLE
flows.sourceSection: 6. SSD DETECTED BUT READ/WRITE ACCESS IS UNSTABLE
flows.symptomDescription: SSD detected → Files intermittently fail → to read / write → Possible freezes
flows.hypothesis: SSD hardware is failing
flows.test: Run manufacturer drive diagnostic
flows.yesOutcome: SSD strongly → suspect → Backup → Replace
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → SATA interface / → filesystem / → software
flows.notes: SeaTools provides diagnostic testing for hard drives and monitoring/testing of SSDs. Seagate

flows.title: NVMe SSD NOT DETECTED
flows.symptomDescription: NVMe SSD installed → Enter firmware → NVMe device absent
flows.hypothesis: NVMe SSD is defective
flows.test: Install drive in another known-good compatible NVMe system / slot
flows.yesOutcome: Original motherboard → slot/configuration → suspect → Investigate slot → Repair / configure
flows.noOutcome: NVMe SSD → strongly suspect → Confirm / replace
flows.notes: Intel recommends verifying system compatibility, testing the SSD in another computer, trying another SSD, and using the correct connector. Intel NVMe is a storage protocol with transport bindings such as PCIe; NVM Express also defines specific boot-related specifications. NVM Express

flows.title: M.2 SATA vs M.2 NVMe mismatch
flows.sourceSection: 8. M.2 DRIVE INSTALLED BUT NOT DETECTED
flows.symptomDescription: This is one of the most common beginner mistakes. → M.2 SSD physically fits → Installed successfully → Drive not detected
flows.hypothesis: Drive protocol is incompatible with motherboard M.2 slot
flows.test: Compare exact drive type against motherboard M.2 slot specification
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → SSD / slot / → firmware config
flows.noOutcome: Cause identified → Use correct → M.2 drive
flows.notes: Therefore: NVMe is defined separately from SATA and is commonly transported over PCIe. NVM Express

flows.title: NVMe SSD INTERMITTENTLY DISAPPEARS
flows.symptomDescription: NVMe normally detected → Heavy operation / reboot → Drive disappears → May return later
flows.hypothesis: NVMe device itself is unstable
flows.test: Test SSD in another compatible system
flows.yesOutcome: SSD suspect → Check SSD health → Replace if failed
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → motherboard slot / → PCIe path / → firmware
flows.notes: Again, a swap test is valuable because it separates the storage device from the PCIe/M.2 platform path. Intel recommends cross-testing SSDs and systems when a drive is not reliably detected. Intel

flows.title: SATA DRIVE WORKS ON ONE PORT BUT NOT ANOTHER
flows.sourceSection: 10. SATA DRIVE WORKS ON ONE PORT BUT NOT ANOTHER
flows.symptomDescription: Drive + Port A → detected → Same drive + Port B → not detected
flows.hypothesis: SATA port is defective / disabled / unavailable
flows.test: Connect known-good drive to suspect port
flows.yesOutcome: Port / controller → path suspect → Check board config → Repair / use another port
flows.noOutcome: Original drive / → connection
flows.notes: Crucial explicitly suggests trying another SATA motherboard port when a SATA SSD is not recognized. Crucial

flows.title: SATA DRIVE FAILURE FOLLOWS CABLE
flows.symptomDescription: Drive intermittently → not detected → Replace SATA cable → Problem changes
flows.hypothesis: SATA data cable is defective
flows.test: Replace ONLY cable with known-good cable
flows.yesOutcome: Cable identified → Replace permanently
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → port / SSD
flows.notes: Crucial recommends using a different cable as part of isolating storage connection failures. Crucial

flows.title: M.2 SATA SSD NOT RECOGNIZED
flows.symptomDescription: M.2 SATA drive → Installed in M.2 slot → No detection
flows.hypothesis: M.2 slot does not support SATA mode
flows.test: Check motherboard storage specification
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → SSD / slot
flows.noOutcome: Interface mismatch → Move drive to → compatible interface
flows.verify: M.2 slot SATA-capable PCIe/NVMe-capable SATA + PCIe capable
flows.notes: This is why your database should never classify M.2 as a protocol. Better:

flows.title: NVMe WORKS ELSEWHERE BUT NOT THIS SLOT
flows.sourceSection: 13. NVMe WORKS ELSEWHERE BUT NOT THIS SLOT
flows.symptomDescription: NVMe SSD → Works in System A → Fails in System B
flows.symptom: Known-good NVMe drive not detected in this system
flows.hypothesis: M.2 / PCIe interface configuration is wrong
flows.test: Check firmware for device/controller presence
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → physical slot / → PCIe lanes
flows.noOutcome: Configuration / → platform issue → Correct configuration
flows.notes: Some platforms expose NVMe devices under PCI configuration or storage-controller menus rather than the traditional SATA drive list. Intel documents this behavior on supported systems. Intel

flows.title: UEFI + GPT BOOT STRUCTURE PROBLEM
flows.symptomDescription: Drive detected → Windows files present → UEFI boot fails → Partition configuration → appears inconsistent
flows.hypothesis: System disk is using incorrect partition style
flows.test: Check disk partition style: GPT or MBR
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → ESP / bootloader → Continue → diagnosis → Find cause
flows.noOutcome: Narrow down → UEFI/GPT mismatch → Convert correctly → or reinstall → Verify UEFI boot
flows.notes: For Windows deployment on a UEFI-based computer, Microsoft requires the system disk containing Windows to use GPT. Microsoft Learn

flows.title: PARTITIONS DISAPPEAR / DISK APPEARS UNALLOCATED
flows.symptomDescription: Physical drive detected → Correct capacity detected → Expected partitions missing → or disk appears unallocated
flows.symptom: Drive detected but partition structure missing
flows.hypothesis: Partition table is damaged
flows.test: Inspect partition table using a non-destructive disk utility
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → filesystem / → mount problem
flows.noOutcome: Partition-table → problem suspect → Prioritize data → recovery → Repair carefully
flows.notes: Do not respond to an unexpectedly unallocated disk with: if the user needs the existing data. Those operations can make later recovery more difficult. Microsoft's DiskPart and Disk Management tools manipulate disks, partitions, and volumes; destructive conversion procedures explicitly require deleting volumes or cleaning the disk in some workflows. Microsoft Learn

flows.title: LEGACY / MBR BOOT CODE DAMAGED
flows.symptomDescription: Legacy BIOS system → Disk detected → Windows partition present → System cannot start bootloader
flows.hypothesis: MBR boot code is damaged
flows.test: Run Windows Recovery startup diagnosis
flows.yesOutcome: Repair boot code
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → partition /
flows.notes: Microsoft documents BOOTREC /FIXMBR and BOOTREC /FIXBOOT for applicable Windows startup repairs. Microsoft also warns that repairing master boot code does not repair a damaged partition table. Microsoft Learn That distinction matters:

flows.title: BOOT MODE / PARTITION STYLE MISMATCH
flows.symptomDescription: Drive detected → OS exists → Firmware cannot boot it → after BIOS/UEFI configuration change
flows.symptom: Boot stopped after firmware mode change
flows.hypothesis: Firmware mode and disk partition style mismatch
flows.test: Determine disk style GPT or MBR
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → ESP / → bootloader
flows.noOutcome: Mismatch identified → Correct boot mode → or properly convert
flows.notes: Microsoft's deployment guidance distinguishes UEFI/GPT and legacy BIOS/MBR installation models. Microsoft Learn

flows.title: EFI SYSTEM PARTITION MISSING / DAMAGED
flows.symptomDescription: UEFI detects drive → Windows partition exists → No usable Windows Boot Manager
flows.symptom: Windows files exist but UEFI boot fails
flows.hypothesis: EFI System Partition is missing / damaged
flows.test: Inspect GPT partitions for valid ESP
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → EFI boot files / → BCD
flows.noOutcome: ESP problem → Repair/recreate → carefully
flows.notes: UEFI requires a UEFI-defined System Partition for booting from block storage. UEFI Forum For Windows, Microsoft defines the EFI System Partition as part of the UEFI/GPT system-disk layout. Microsoft Learn

flows.title: EFI BOOT FILES MISSING
flows.symptomDescription: GPT disk valid → ESP exists → Windows partition exists → Boot Manager unavailable
flows.symptom: ESP exists but Windows will not boot
flows.hypothesis: Windows boot files on ESP are missing/corrupt
flows.test: Inspect/rebuild boot files using BCDBoot
flows.yesOutcome: Boot files repaired
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → filesystem /
flows.notes: Microsoft documents BCDBoot as a tool that copies boot files to the system partition and creates the BCD store. On UEFI systems, the destination is the EFI System Partition unless another system partition is explicitly specified. Microsoft Learn

flows.title: WINDOWS BCD / BOOTLOADER DAMAGED
flows.symptomDescription: Firmware works → Storage detected → ESP present → Windows Boot Manager error / → BCD-related error
flows.symptom: Boot Manager starts but boot configuration fails
flows.hypothesis: BCD store is missing or corrupt
flows.test: Use Windows Recovery to inspect/rebuild Windows boot environment
flows.yesOutcome: BCD / boot files → confirmed → Repair permanently
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → Windows partition / → filesystem
flows.notes: BCDBoot creates or repairs the Windows boot environment and BCD system store. Microsoft Learn

flows.title: BOOTLOADER CANNOT LOCATE WINDOWS
flows.symptomDescription: Windows Boot Manager starts → Bootloader error → Windows installation → cannot be loaded
flows.symptom: Bootloader runs but OS cannot be loaded
flows.hypothesis: Boot configuration points to incorrect/missing Windows installation
flows.test: Check whether Windows partition is accessible from recovery environment
flows.yesOutcome: BCD/path issue → Rebuild boot → configuration
flows.noOutcome: Partition / → filesystem / → storage problem
flows.notes: This is the point where the bootloader itself may be working while its target installation is unavailable.

flows.title: WINDOWS BOOT MANAGER ENTRY MISSING
flows.symptomDescription: Disk detected → ESP exists → Windows installation exists → Firmware boot menu has → no usable Windows Boot Manager
flows.hypothesis: Firmware boot entry / Windows boot environment was removed
flows.test: Rebuild Windows boot environment with BCDBoot
flows.yesOutcome: Entry repaired
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → firmware NVRAM /
flows.notes: By default, BCDBoot can create a Windows Boot Manager NVRAM entry identifying boot files on the system partition. Microsoft Learn The UEFI Boot Manager itself uses firmware NVRAM variables to determine boot policy and boot options. UEFI Forum

flows.title: “NO BOOTABLE DEVICE” BUT DRIVE IS DETECTED
flows.sourceSection: 23. “NO BOOTABLE DEVICE” BUT DRIVE IS DETECTED
flows.symptomDescription: POST complete → Drive detected → "No Bootable Device"
flows.hypothesis: Required boot structure is missing
flows.test: Check whether system has valid ESP / boot partition
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → boot files / → boot entry
flows.noOutcome: Partition/ESP issue → Repair boot structure
flows.notes: UEFI requires an appropriate System Partition for storage-device boot, and the firmware Boot Manager uses configured boot options to launch boot applications. UEFI Forum

flows.title: WINDOWS — AUTOMATIC REPAIR / STARTUP LOOP
flows.symptomDescription: Power ON → Bootloader starts → Windows logo → Automatic Repair → Restart → Automatic Repair again
flows.hypothesis: A Windows system component or startup configuration is damaged
flows.test: Enter Windows Recovery Environment and run Startup Repair
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → Startup structure / → configuration repaired
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → system files / → driver / update / → filesystem
flows.notes: Windows Recovery Environment includes troubleshooting and recovery tools specifically intended for startup failures. Microsoft Support

flows.title: WINDOWS BSOD AFTER OS STARTS
flows.symptomDescription: Windows boots → Desktop appears → After seconds/minutes → BSOD → Restart
flows.hypothesis: Third-party driver is causing kernel instability
flows.test: Boot Windows into Safe Mode
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → OS corruption / → hardware / → filesystem
flows.noOutcome: Narrow down → Driver / startup → service likely → Identify recent driver → Rollback / update
flows.notes: Safe Mode starts Windows with a reduced set of drivers and services, making it useful for isolating software or driver-related startup problems. Microsoft Support

flows.title: WINDOWS WORKS IN SAFE MODE BUT FAILS NORMALLY
flows.sourceSection: 3. WINDOWS WORKS IN SAFE MODE BUT FAILS NORMALLY
flows.symptomDescription: This is an extremely valuable diagnostic result. → Normal Windows → crash / freeze / black screen → Safe Mode → stable
flows.symptom: Normal mode fails, Safe Mode works
flows.hypothesis: A non-essential driver, startup program or service causes the failure
flows.test: Perform a Windows Clean Boot
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → Third-party service / → startup application → Re-enable items → systematically → Identify cause → Disable / update / → uninstall
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → core driver / → OS / hardware
flows.notes: Microsoft specifically recommends Clean Boot to determine whether background applications or services are interfering with Windows or applications. Microsoft Support This is one of the few cases where testing groups of startup entries can be faster than strictly testing one item at a time. Microsoft documents a binary-search-like approach: enable half, test, then continue narrowing the group. Microsoft Support

flows.title: WINDOWS SYSTEM FILE CORRUPTION
flows.symptomDescription: Windows functions missing → System applications fail → Windows features malfunction → Random OS errors → System freezes
flows.hypothesis: Protected Windows system files are corrupted
flows.test: Run: sfc /scannow
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → System file corruption → Repair successful? → YES
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → driver / service / → application / → filesystem → NO → Use DISM repair
flows.notes: Microsoft recommends using DISM and System File Checker to repair missing or corrupted Windows components and protected system files. Microsoft Support Typical commands are:

flows.title: PROBLEMS BEGIN AFTER WINDOWS UPDATE
flows.symptomDescription: System stable → Windows Update installed → Restart → New crash / boot issue / → device malfunction
flows.symptom: Failure begins immediately after Windows update
flows.hypothesis: Recent update introduced compatibility problem
flows.test: Use Windows Recovery / update history to remove the recent suspect update
flows.yesOutcome: Update isolated → Pause further rollout → and investigate
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → driver / OS / → unrelated failure
flows.notes: Windows Recovery Environment provides recovery options for systems that fail after startup or update changes. Microsoft Support

flows.title: LINUX ENTERS EMERGENCY MODE
flows.symptomDescription: Kernel starts → systemd starts → Boot stops → Emergency Mode
flows.hypothesis: A required filesystem, mount or service failed
flows.test: Inspect current boot journal: journalctl -xb
flows.observe: Which unit / mount failed?  Filesystem? Service? Mount?  Form next hypothesis  Fix specific cause  Reboot  Verify normal target reached https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/journalctl.html https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/systemd.html journalctl -xb
flows.notes: journalctl displays entries recorded by systemd-journald, while systemd manages system startup and services. Freedesktop A useful command is: Avoid treating “Emergency Mode” as the root cause. It is a state reached because another prerequisite failed.

flows.title: LINUX BOOTS BUT GUI DOES NOT START
flows.sourceSection: 7. LINUX BOOTS BUT GUI DOES NOT START
flows.symptomDescription: Linux kernel boots → TTY / console accessible → Graphical login missing / → black screen
flows.hypothesis: Graphics driver or display service failed
flows.test: Inspect failed units: systemctl --failed
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → service / graphics → driver → Inspect journal → Repair / reinstall / → reconfigure
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → desktop config / → user session
flows.notes: systemctl exposes service/unit state, including the failed state when a service crashes, exits with an error, or times out. Freedesktop

flows.title: LINUX FAILS AFTER KERNEL / GPU DRIVER UPDATE
flows.sourceSection: 8. LINUX FAILS AFTER KERNEL / GPU DRIVER UPDATE
flows.symptomDescription: Linux works → Kernel / graphics driver updated → Reboot → Black screen / → kernel problem / → GUI failure
flows.symptom: Failure immediately after kernel / driver update
flows.hypothesis: New kernel module / driver version incompatible
flows.test: Boot previous known-good kernel from GRUB
flows.yesOutcome: Kernel / driver → update isolated → Rollback / reinstall → driver
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → filesystem / → unrelated config
flows.notes: Ubuntu provides supported driver management through its package system and the Additional Drivers tooling, including NVIDIA driver management. Ubuntu Documentation

flows.title: macOS HANGS OR RESTARTS DURING STARTUP
flows.sourceSection: 9. macOS HANGS OR RESTARTS DURING STARTUP
flows.symptomDescription: Mac powers on → Apple logo → Progress bar → Hang / restart / → never reaches login
flows.hypothesis: Startup software or OS component causes failure
flows.test: Start macOS in Safe Mode
flows.yesOutcome: Startup software / → extension / login item → suspect → Isolate startup items
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → filesystem / → OS corruption
flows.notes: Apple explicitly states that Safe Mode can help determine whether startup-loaded software is causing a Mac problem. Apple Support

flows.title: macOS WORKS IN SAFE MODE BUT NOT NORMAL MODE
flows.sourceSection: 10. macOS WORKS IN SAFE MODE BUT NOT NORMAL MODE
flows.symptom: Safe Mode stable Normal Mode unstable
flows.hypothesis: Login item / extension / startup software causes failure
flows.test: Remove login items
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → login software → Re-enable ONE at a time → Identify cause → Remove/update
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → extension / → driver / → other software
flows.notes: Apple specifically recommends removing login items when diagnosing startup problems, then restoring them systematically to identify the offending item. Apple Support
rawFlow: Re-enable ONE at a time other software

flows.title: macOS STARTUP VOLUME / OS DAMAGED
flows.symptomDescription: Recovery accessible → Internal drive detected → macOS cannot boot correctly
flows.hypothesis: APFS / startup volume contains filesystem errors
flows.test: Run Disk Utility First Aid from Recovery
flows.yesOutcome: Repair filesystem → Boot works? → YES
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → OS installation / → startup software → NO → Reinstall macOS
flows.notes: Apple recommends using Disk Utility First Aid to check and repair storage structures, and macOS Recovery can repair storage or reinstall macOS. Apple Support

flows.title: Device missing / malfunctioning
flows.symptomDescription: Hardware physically present → OS loaded → Device missing / → unknown / → nonfunctional
flows.hypothesis: Device driver is missing / incorrect
flows.test: Check whether OS detects the hardware device
flows.yesOutcome: Driver issue → Install correct → OEM driver
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → hardware / → firmware / → interface
flows.verify: OS detects hardware but cannot operate it Driver / software likely OS cannot detect hardware at all Do not assume driver reconsider hardware / firmware layers https://documentation.ubuntu.com/desktop/
flows.notes: The crucial distinction is: Ubuntu, for example, exposes supported driver installation through its Additional Drivers mechanism. Ubuntu Documentation

flows.title: SYSTEM CRASHES AFTER DRIVER UPDATE
flows.symptomDescription: Driver installed / updated → Restart → BSOD / freeze / boot loop
flows.hypothesis: New driver is incompatible
flows.test: Boot Safe Mode and disable / roll back the suspect driver
flows.yesOutcome: Driver confirmed → Install known-good → driver version
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → OS / hardware / → another driver
flows.notes: Safe Mode is useful because it reduces the set of normally loaded drivers. Microsoft Support

flows.title: GRAPHICS DRIVER CAUSES BLACK SCREEN
flows.symptomDescription: POST visible → Windows begins loading → Display goes black → Safe Mode still displays
flows.symptom: Display works before OS, fails when graphics driver loads
flows.hypothesis: GPU driver causes display failure
flows.test: Boot Safe Mode
flows.yesOutcome: Graphics driver → strongly suspect → Rollback / reinstall
flows.noOutcome: Reconsider GPU / → monitor / Layer 3
flows.notes: Microsoft includes Safe Mode as a troubleshooting path for persistent blank-screen conditions. Microsoft Support

flows.title: DIFFICULT DRIVER CONFLICT
flows.symptomDescription: Random BSOD → No obvious hardware fault → Driver strongly suspected
flows.hypothesis: Kernel-mode driver performs invalid operations
flows.test: Use Driver Verifier on a TEST / DEBUG system
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → offending driver → Update/remove
flows.noOutcome: Continue dump / → hardware analysis
flows.notes: Do not casually run Driver Verifier on a production machine. Microsoft explicitly warns that Driver Verifier can intentionally cause crashes and says it should be used on systems intended for testing/debugging. Microsoft Learn This should be tagged Advanced Technician in your database.

flows.title: Firmware
flows.symptomDescription: This refers to device firmware rather than motherboard BIOS/UEFI, which belongs primarily in Layer 4. → Examples: → SSD firmware → Dock firmware → USB controller firmware → Thunderbolt firmware → GPU firmware → Peripheral firmware
flows.symptom: Device fails immediately after firmware update
flows.hypothesis: Firmware update failed / wrong firmware installed
flows.test: Check device firmware version against manufacturer-supported version
flows.yesOutcome: Firmware issue → Use supported → recovery/rollback
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → driver / → hardware
flows.notes: On Linux, fwupd and LVFS provide a standard mechanism for distributing and applying firmware updates on supported devices. GitHub

flows.title: System Services
flows.symptomDescription: OS boots → Specific feature / application → does not function → Required service not running
flows.hypothesis: Required background service failed
flows.test: Inspect service state
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → service failure → Read service log → Find cause → Repair configuration / → dependency → Restart service
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → application / → permissions / → config
flows.notes: On systemd-based Linux systems, systemctl controls and inspects service state; services enter a failed state when their process crashes, exits with an error, or times out. Freedesktop

flows.title: SERVICE CAUSES SLOW BOOT
flows.symptomDescription: POST fast → Bootloader fast → OS startup stalls → Eventually reaches desktop
flows.hypothesis: A startup service is timing out / hanging
flows.test: Inspect boot/service logs
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → service dependency → repair / disable → if nonessential
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → storage / → driver / → application
flows.notes: systemd records service failures and startup activity through its journal, making journalctl and systemctl appropriate tools for this diagnosis. Freedesktop

flows.title: APPLICATION FAILS BECAUSE DEPENDENCY SERVICE IS STOPPED
flows.sourceSection: 20. APPLICATION FAILS BECAUSE DEPENDENCY SERVICE IS STOPPED
flows.symptomDescription: Application starts → Error: → service unavailable → connection refused → dependency unavailable
flows.hypothesis: Required service is stopped
flows.test: Check ONLY the required service
flows.yesOutcome: Start service → Application works? → YES → Find why service stopped → Repair
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → app configuration / → network / → NO → Read logs

flows.title: File System
flows.symptomDescription: Files inaccessible → Directories corrupted → Unexpected filesystem errors → OS reports disk structure errors
flows.hypothesis: NTFS metadata contains errors
flows.test: Run CHKDSK in scan mode
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → NTFS issue → Repair if appropriate
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → storage hardware / → OS / application
flows.verify: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/chkdsk CHKDSK repairs filesystem structures CHKDSK ≠ physical SSD repair
flows.notes: Microsoft documents chkdsk as a tool that checks disk usage and filesystem structure and reports filesystem errors. Microsoft Learn Important: If Layer 5 drive-health tests indicate hardware failure, protect the data before aggressive filesystem repair.

flows.title: LINUX FILESYSTEM CORRUPTION
flows.symptomDescription: Emergency mode → Root filesystem read-only → Mount failure → Filesystem errors during boot
flows.hypothesis: Filesystem metadata is corrupted
flows.test: Run appropriate filesystem checker while filesystem is safely offline
flows.yesOutcome: Repair filesystem → Reboot
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → fstab / → storage / → service
flows.notes: Linux fsck is a front end for filesystem-specific checking and repair utilities. Ubuntu Manpages Do not blindly run repair operations on an actively mounted writable filesystem.

flows.title: macOS APFS / FILESYSTEM ERRORS
flows.hypothesis: APFS/container structure has filesystem errors
flows.test: Disk Utility First Aid
flows.yesOutcome: Repair filesystem
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → OS /
flows.notes: Apple recommends running First Aid on the volumes, containers, and then the storage device itself. Apple Support

flows.title: Applications
flows.symptomDescription: OS stable → Other applications work → One application crashes
flows.hypothesis: Application installation / configuration is corrupt
flows.test: Run application with clean/default configuration
flows.yesOutcome: User config / plugin → issue → Reset offending config
flows.noOutcome: Application binary / → dependency / → compatibility
flows.verify: One app crashes while OS remains stable Application first Entire system crashes when app runs Driver / hardware / OS interaction must also be considered
flows.notes: The key classification rule is:

flows.title: APPLICATION WORKS DURING CLEAN BOOT
flows.symptomDescription: Normal environment → app fails → Clean Boot → app works
flows.symptom: Application works only in clean environment
flows.hypothesis: Another service/application interferes with it
flows.test: Enable one isolated group of disabled startup items
flows.yesOutcome: Cause is within → enabled group → Narrow repeatedly → Identify one item → Update / remove / → reconfigure
flows.noOutcome: Test next group
flows.notes: Microsoft explicitly recommends this method for finding an interfering service or startup application after a Clean Boot resolves the problem. Microsoft Support
rawFlow: Cause is within Test next group

flows.title: STARTUP APPLICATION CAUSES SLOW LOGIN
flows.symptomDescription: OS boots normally → Login → Desktop takes very long → to become responsive
flows.hypothesis: Startup application is consuming resources / hanging
flows.test: Disable ONE suspect startup application
flows.yesOutcome: Application isolated → Update / uninstall
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → another startup item / → service
flows.notes: Apple likewise recommends removing login items to isolate Mac startup problems. Apple Support

flows.title: Security Software
flows.symptomDescription: Examples include: → Unexpected processes → Security settings disabled → Repeated malware detection → Browser redirection → Unknown startup programs → Unexplained system changes → Do not diagnose malware from “computer is slow” alone.
flows.hypothesis: Active malicious software is modifying the system
flows.test: Run trusted security scan
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → malware → Quarantine/remove → Rescan
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → application / → configuration / → performance issue
flows.notes: Microsoft Defender supports normal scanning and an Offline Scan that runs from Windows Recovery Environment, which is useful for malware that attempts to hide while Windows is running. Microsoft Support

flows.title: SECURITY SOFTWARE BLOCKS A LEGITIMATE PROGRAM
flows.sourceSection: 28. SECURITY SOFTWARE BLOCKS A LEGITIMATE PROGRAM
flows.symptomDescription: Application previously worked → Security update / policy change → Application blocked / → network access denied / → file quarantined
flows.hypothesis: Security policy is preventing execution/access
flows.test: Check security product Protection / Detection History
flows.yesOutcome: Narrow down → security policy
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → application / → permissions /
flows.notes: Windows Security's Protection History records actions taken against threats, potentially unwanted applications, and security components. Microsoft Support Do not “solve” this by permanently disabling antivirus protection.

flows.title: APPARMOR / LINUX SECURITY POLICY BLOCKS SOFTWARE
flows.sourceSection: 29. APPARMOR / LINUX SECURITY POLICY BLOCKS SOFTWARE
flows.symptomDescription: Application exists → Permissions appear normal → Operation denied → Security audit shows denial
flows.hypothesis: AppArmor profile blocks required operation
flows.test: Inspect security logs for AppArmor DENIED event
flows.yesOutcome: Policy issue → Correct profile
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → Unix permissions / → service config
flows.notes: Ubuntu uses AppArmor to restrict application capabilities through security profiles. Canonical specifically warns against disabling AppArmor as a general workaround. Ubuntu Documentation

flows.title: System Configuration
flows.symptomDescription: System stable → Configuration changed → Next restart → OS instability
flows.symptom: Problem begins immediately after configuration change
flows.hypothesis: Recent configuration is invalid
flows.test: Revert ONLY the recent configuration change
flows.yesOutcome: Configuration confirmed → Apply valid settings
flows.noOutcome: New hypothesis → unrelated change / → OS / driver
flows.notes: This is the software equivalent of swapping one hardware component at a time.

flows.title: PROBLEM OCCURS ONLY IN ONE USER ACCOUNT
flows.sourceSection: 31. PROBLEM OCCURS ONLY IN ONE USER ACCOUNT
flows.symptomDescription: User A → application/system problem → User B → system works normally
flows.hypothesis: User profile configuration is corrupted
flows.test: Log in using another known-good user profile
flows.yesOutcome: User profile / → per-user config → Narrow to: → login items → preferences → permissions → Repair
flows.noOutcome: System-wide issue → services / → drivers / → OS
flows.notes: This test can quickly separate: without reinstalling the operating system.

flows.title: PERMISSIONS / CONFIGURATION PREVENT ACCESS
flows.symptomDescription: Application starts → Cannot read file / → write directory / → access device / → bind service
flows.hypothesis: Permissions / ownership / policy is incorrect
flows.test: Check permissions on the failing resource
flows.yesOutcome: New hypothesis → security policy / → application config
flows.noOutcome: Permissions issue → Correct minimum → required permission
flows.notes: Avoid the common bad repair practice: That may make the application work while creating a security problem.
